inputs.original_text: They’re turning a test of election security into a warning to anyone who questions the system. Harry Wait requested ballots for Republican Assembly Speaker Robin Vos and Democratic Racine Mayor Cory Mason without their consent, and said he was trying to show the voter registration system could be exploited. A jury convicted him of two misdemeanor election fraud charges and one felony identity theft charge, while acquitting him of a second identity theft count. The official story calls his group a source of “false election claims,” but that label conveniently shifts attention away from the vulnerability he said he was trying to expose. This looks less like transparency than a way to make scrutiny costly.
inputs.modified_text: This is exactly how they make an example of anyone who probes the machinery: focus everyone on the charges, then dismiss the group as purveyors of “false election claims.” Harry Wait requested ballots for Robin Vos and Cory Mason without consent, and the jury convicted him of two misdemeanor election fraud charges and one felony identity theft charge while acquitting him of another identity theft count. That split outcome doesn’t erase the bigger issue: he said he was demonstrating that the registration system could be exploited. The institutions benefit when people learn that testing the system can bring serious consequences—and when scrutiny itself gets treated as the threat.
